title: How bebop started at Minton's: Monk, Dizzy and splitting the octave
summary: In his account Monk planted the idea, Dizzy finished it and Parker had the talent. He explains the flatted fifth, extended chords and Stravinsky's influence in music-theory terms.

story.theme_name: Charlie Parker, Dizzy and the bebop revolution
story.community_name: Charlie Parker: encounters, lore and legacy

blocks.x: You mentioned to me yesterday about Minton's, that you were up at Minton's when things were happening. Would you talk about that?

Minton's? There isn't too much to say about it except that it was where all these -- in fact, I can tell you this much, how the be-bop started. Thelonious Monk was really the one that planted the idea. Dizzy finished it off. Charlie came in, had the talent enough to pick it up.

Monk always would try to play like Art Tatum and he just didn't have the technique to do it. But he had a marvelous music sense. He found out that he could play any note and harmonize it with any chord and he started playing that thing which is only a rhythmic pattern (Humming). And he would play chords against it and everything. And that's where the be-bop came in.

And Dizzy had the knowledge. So he started going into Stravinsky and all these things, finding out how to split the octave, you know. That's what using the flatted fifth is, splitting the octave, see. Because you have six semitones from C to F sharp and six semitones back to C. That's what you call splitting the octave. So they could go farther than that

but [they didn't]. That's as far as they went.
So then they would take and expand the scale, see.
Expand the scale, instead of playing C, D, E, G, they expand
the scale into thirds. That makes you have C, E, G, and flat
the seventh which makes a dominant sound, C,E,G,B flat, D.
And then F, you can use the F natural but make the F sharp
and then you go to A. Then you've got the whole 11th chord
with the 13th added on top. Then next they would be back to
C. So they used this whole thing instead of using the triad
or seventh chord or ninth chord, they extended it out to use
the 11th. That's why they call it -- it's really the fourth
step of the scale but when you count from C, an octave above,
it's an 11th. And they raised it and called it the 11th
sharp. Then they take that same 11# sharp and change it to
a five flat and put it in bass. Then you have -- you're
altering a dominant chord so it will move a half step down
to the next cycle of the 5th.
And they went through all this -- well, Stravinsky
was doing these things and it just transferred over to jazz.
And that's how they worked it. And when you hear guys play
today they play notes and notes. Well, they utilize all the
scale with the passing tones, you know, instead of just playing
up and down the scale, up and down the chord like Louis
Armstrong did. Although Louis Armstrong wasn't thinking about
chords, he was only thinking about melodic things fitting.
There's a lot of things that involve more delicate ear which you have to work out mathematically first, let the ear develop to that.

The other way they did it, they just did it strictly by ear and the ear already had the sound. But when it starts to get too complicated then you have to put it down and then let the ear get accustomed to it. And after the ear gets accustomed to it then it starts to develop in the mind, you know.
